name: Noname
label: Self-released
lede: A Bronzeville bookstore kid who made a mixtape in two rented Airbnbs, ran a book club that ships to prisons, and put out her second album on her own terms in 2023.

eras.title: A bookstore kid from Bronzeville
eras.text: Fatimah Warner grew up on Chicago's South Side, hung around her mother's Afrocentric bookstore, and found her way to poetry before she found rap. The Chicago scene she came up in (YOUMedia, slam, open mics) is where her circle formed.

years.h: Born in Bronzeville to a family of readers and shopkeepers
years.p: Fatimah Nyeema Warner is raised by her grandparents, both entrepreneurs, until middle school, then moves in with her mother, who owns an Afrocentric bookstore.
years.xp: According to Wikipedia, she listened to the blues players Buddy Guy and Howlin' Wolf as a teenager and spent hours in her mother's shop. The bookstore later closed, and she has pointed to that loss when explaining why her own book club backs independent sellers.

years.h: Slam poet at the library, rapper as Noname Gypsy
years.p: She starts rapping under the name Noname Gypsy, after a high school creative writing class turns her toward poetry. Third place at Louder Than a Bomb, Chicago's teen slam festival.
years.xp: She spent time at YOUMedia, the teen digital-arts space inside the Harold Washington Library. That is where she befriended [[Chance the Rapper|373a4c98-a46b-48e4-86ec-f6ca65b4f438]] and met the experimental rapper LUCKI, per Wikipedia.

eras.title: The guest verse everyone rewound
eras.text: Before she had a project of her own, Noname was the voice people kept finding inside other people's records. Chicago's mixtape class of the early 2010s put her on speed dial.

years.h: 'Lost' on Acid Rap, then The Waters, then Late Knight Special
years.p: Her verse on 'Lost' from [[Chance the Rapper|373a4c98-a46b-48e4-86ec-f6ca65b4f438]]'s Acid Rap in 2013 is her first wide exposure. Mick Jenkins's The Waters follows in 2014 and Kirk Knight's Late Knight Special in 2015.

eras.title: Telefone, and a name with nothing attached
eras.text: The mixtape she had been announcing since 2012 finally lands, free, and Chicago's new soul-rap wave has a face. She also drops the word 'Gypsy' for good.

years.h: Noname Gypsy becomes just Noname
years.p: She drops 'Gypsy' after learning the word is a slur for Romani people. The new name, she says, is about not being boxed in.
years.xp: Wikipedia quotes her explaining the change: 'Noname could potentially be a nurse. Noname could be a screenwriter.' The mixtape she was working on had already been announced under the old name in 2012.

years.h: Telefone · free on Bandcamp after four years of delays
years.p: Ten tracks, phone calls as a device, and guests including [[Saba|057d211a-fba8-42d7-ad14-41f41d6f762f]], [[Smino|96800e05-9924-4321-859a-76e0d4750f2f]] and Eryn Allen Kane. Pitchfork called it a 'stunning debut' and gave it 8.0.
years.xp:
Wikipedia says Noname told an interviewer in January 2014 that finishing depended on whether she could afford mixing. In June 2016 she moved to Los Angeles with her production team and set up makeshift studios in two Airbnb rentals to finish it. [[Phoelix|c9a8ee10-c27e-4b78-90a9-0b5a230e7941]] and Cam O'bi were the executive producers, with [[Saba|057d211a-fba8-42d7-ad14-41f41d6f762f]] and Monte Booker also producing.

Pitchfork ranked it No. 27 among its 50 best albums of 2016, and Stereogum put it at No. 28. The cover was hand-painted by Nikko Washington of the Chicago collective SaveMoney. Vinyl pressings came in September 2017.

years.h: Saturday Night Live, on Chance the Rapper's night
years.p: Noname appears with [[Chance the Rapper|373a4c98-a46b-48e4-86ec-f6ca65b4f438]] on SNL in December 2016, five months after Telefone.

yt: Diddy Bop, live at Fader Fort 2017
years.h: NPR Tiny Desk: five Telefone songs and a four-piece band
years.p: She plays 'Diddy Bop', 'Yesterday', 'Reality Check', 'Casket Pretty' and 'Bye Bye Baby'.

eras.title: Room 25, and a second job
eras.text: Noname makes the album everyone waits for, then starts a book club that turns into the more consuming project. The second album gets announced and then does not arrive.

years.h: Room 25: recorded in one summer, paid for with tour money
years.p: Named for the hotel rooms she lived in at 25 in Los Angeles. Pitchfork gave it 8.6 and Best New Music.
years.xp:
Wikipedia dates the recording to July through September 2018, with [[Phoelix|c9a8ee10-c27e-4b78-90a9-0b5a230e7941]] as principal producer and Luke Titus and Brian Sanborn on select tracks. It was self-funded from touring proceeds. Noname told The Fader: 'I needed to make an album because I need to pay my rent.'

Pitchfork's Briana Younger called it 'a transcendent coming-of-age tale built around cosmic jazz and neo-soul.' Pitchfork ranked it No. 15 of 2018, and Robert Christgau later called it the fifth-best album of the 2010s.

years.h: Room 25 on The Late Show with Stephen Colbert
years.p: Network TV, about a month after release.

years.h: Factory Baby is announced as her next album
years.p: Two and a half years later, she will cancel it. Noname says she struggled to find producers she connected with sonically.

years.cap: Die US-amerikanische Rapperin Noname beim splash! Festival 20 (2017). · Wikimedia
years.h: Noname Book Club starts with a fan reading Jackson Rising
years.p: Its first picks are Paulo Freire's Pedagogy of the Oppressed and Samantha Irby's We Are Never Meeting in Real Life.
years.xp:
Wikipedia says the club began when a fan noted they were reading the same book she was. It picks two books a month and steers readers toward local, POC-owned bookstores. Noname described it as 'a little bit of a fuck you to Amazon', per Wikipedia.

By 2023, Wikipedia counts donations to more than 400 prison facilities. The Mary Sue reports the Prison Program ships over 600 books a month.

years.h: Ghetto Sage: Noname, Saba and Smino, one song
years.p: The trio drop 'Häagen Dazs' in October 2019. They reunite on Noname's Tiny Desk in 2023.

years.h: She says she might quit over who is buying her music
years.p: Noname voices frustration with her largely white audience and considers walking away, according to Wikipedia.
years.xp: Wikipedia quotes her: 'I refuse to keep making music and putting it online for free for people who won't support me.'

eras.title: Less music, more work
eras.text: A stretch defined by what she did not release. Politics, organizing and her book club take over the calendar, and an album is announced, delayed and finally cancelled.

years.h: Library Card Registration Day
years.p: Noname invents a day for people to sign up for a library card, and criticizes Amazon's 'consumer model' while doing it.

years.big: 'My ego got the best of me.'
q: my ego got the best of me
years.h: 'Song 33' answers J. Cole's 'Snow on tha Bluff'
years.p: Two days after J. Cole's song seemed to take a shot at her activism, she puts out a Madlib-produced reply about violence against Black women.
years.xp:
Wikipedia notes the track reflected on Oluwatoyin Salau's death. Noname later wrote she was not proud of responding with it, apologized for the distraction, and said she was leaving it up, per NME. She donated her proceeds to Black mutual aid funds.

NME reports Cole never confirmed the song was about her; he later said he honors her as a leader in the reading and learning.

years.h: She turns down the Judas and the Black Messiah soundtrack
years.p: After seeing the film, Noname declines the offer and criticizes it for not centering Fred Hampton's 'radical communist politics'.

years.h: Radical Hood Library opens in Los Angeles
years.p: The Book Club's free library and prison-book shipping hub prioritizes Black and Brown neighbors for its first RSVPs.

years.cap: Die US-amerikanische Rapperin Noname beim splash! Festival 20 (2017). · Wikimedia
years.h: Factory Baby is cancelled and music goes on hold
years.p: Noname says on Instagram that the album is off and she is taking an indefinite break.
years.xp: She had said earlier that political education and organizing were pulling her away. The Nation quotes her: 'a little less interested in making music.' Her book club had grown into chapters across the US and a prison program.

years.h: Pitchfork Music Festival books her for July
years.p: She posts home-studio photos the next day. In April she is added to Afropunk and says an album would follow a few shows.

eras.title: Sundial, on her own terms
eras.text: Coachella, a controversy over one guest verse, an album and a block party in the neighborhood that raised her. The record lands as Pitchfork's No. 13 of the year.

years.h: She's on the Coachella 2023 lineup
years.p: The first big festival lineup with her name on it since the 2021 cancellation.

years.h: Factory Baby becomes Sundial
years.p: The new record is announced, with a July target. Noname is releasing it herself.

years.src: Wikipedia: Sundial (album) · Wikipedia: Noname (rapper) · The Hurst Review
years.h: Balloons: a lead single pulled after a day
years.p: Noname announces 'Balloons' with [[Jay Electronica|8bf283b9-b1e2-4632-a953-eacd212a543e]] and [[Eryn Allen Kane|8c94a5be-2932-477f-80f8-0a07c850cd78]] for July 21, backlash over Electronica erupts, and the single release is cancelled.
years.xp:
Wikipedia reports the backlash centered on Jay Electronica's antisemitism accusations and his comments about the Ukraine war on the track. She defended the collaboration on Twitter before deleting her account two days later. She contemplated shelving the whole album, per the Sundial article. The track was on the final record anyway.

The Hurst Review's Aug. 17 roundup notes Noname 'has refused calls to apologize'.

q: a cool and masterful interrogation of the culture
years.src: Album of the Year · BrooklynVegan · The Nation · Wikipedia: Sundial (album)
years.h: Sundial is out, self-released, 31 minutes and 50 seconds
years.p: Pitchfork gave it 8.8 and ranked it No. 13 of 2023. Metacritic has it at 87 from nine reviews.
years.xp:
Album of the Year lists Pitchfork's score as 88, from Alphonse Pierre. PopMatters and The Line of Best Fit each gave it 90, Rolling Stone and The Guardian 80, AllMusic 70. The Needle Drop's Anthony Fantano scored it 50. The AOTY critic average was 81 from 11 reviews.

Pitchfork's 2023 year-end list put it at No. 13, between L'Rain's I Killed Your Dog and Olivia Rodrigo's GUTS, per BrooklynVegan. The Nation's Stephen Kearse wrote that it deals with celebrity, radical politics and her own contradictions 'with humility and openness'.

years.h: Eleven tracks, one hominin skull on the cover
years.p: The artwork is based on John Gurche's reconstruction of Homo floresiensis specimen LB1. [[Saba|057d211a-fba8-42d7-ad14-41f41d6f762f]] produced 'Balloons' and 'Toxic'; [[Common|c0a1179b-b14a-4d68-a3c1-1fdab16ed602]] guests on 'Oblivion'.
years.xp: Producers include Daoud, Gaetan Judd, Yussef Dayes with Wesley Singerman on 'Potentially the Interlude', Slimwav on 'Namesake', and Berg on 'Oblivion'. Guests: billy woods and $ilkMoney on 'Gospel?', Ayoni on 'Boomboom' and 'Oblivion', Jimetta Rose and Voices of Creation on 'Hold Me Down'.

years.cap: Noname (Fatimah Warner) performing at Phoenix Concert Theatre as part of the Telefone Tour on March 5, 2017. Toronto, ON, Canada. · Wikimedia
years.h: A Bronzeville block party with Common closing the show
years.p: In a parking lot at 43rd Street and Lake Park Avenue, with Navy Blue, Alex Vaughn and two DJs. Noname played with a live band.
years.xp: CBS Chicago reports there was a supply giveaway. Noname told the station she wanted to celebrate with the community that raised her, and was planning her first Chicago bookstore within the year.

years.h: Tiny Desk, part two, with Smino and Saba for one song
years.p: Six songs, mostly from Sundial. She closes with 'Balloons', which she jokingly calls her 'most controversial song'.
